title: TempLat: a versatile C++ engine for lattice field theories
abstract: We present TempLat, a C++ framework for lattice field theory simulations in arbitrary dimensions. Its symbolic language, built on expression templates, translates mathematical expressions almost verbatim into C++ while compiling to highly optimized kernels, in contexts ranging from classical-statistical to Monte Carlo simulations. TempLat is performance-portable: building on Kokkos, it supports large CPU clusters, as well as NVIDIA and AMD GPUs. Its abstraction of hardware into a device concept makes TempLat extensible to future architectures. We demonstrate excellent strong and weak scaling on both CPUs and GPUs. We also present ParaFaFT, a standalone parallel discrete Fourier transform library supporting arbitrary dimensions on all of the above hardware, and benchmark its scaling. Both are open source and available on GitHub, and power a new release of CosmoLattice, a widely used early-universe simulation library now available on GPUs.
summary: This paper introduces TempLat, a versatile C++ engine designed for high-performance lattice field theory simulations in arbitrary dimensions. It uses advanced techniques like expression templates and Kokkos to ensure portability across CPUs and GPUs while maintaining compile-time optimization. The framework successfully benchmarks complex physics models, demonstrating state-of-the-art scaling performance.
main_problem: The need for an efficient, versatile, and high-performance software framework capable of simulating lattice field theories across various physical regimes.
main_result: TempLat provides a dimension-agnostic C++ engine that achieves excellent strong and weak scaling on both CPU clusters and modern GPUs by decoupling mathematical expressions from hardware implementation.
method: The framework uses expression templates to translate high-level mathematical expressions almost verbatim into highly optimized, device-specific C++ kernels, supporting hybrid MPI/shared-memory parallelization via Kokkos.
model_or_system: It is designed for lattice field theories, simulating systems ranging from QCD and early-universe dynamics ($	ext{SU}(2)$ Yang–Mills) to classical statistical models like the $\phi^4$ theory. It supports various gauge groups and complex field types.
key_observables: Wall-clock time per lattice site per step; scaling behavior (strong/weak); average values of fields ($\langle \phi angle$).
important_parameters: Lattice dimensions ($d$), coupling constants ($\lambda$), simulation time steps ($dt$), and hardware resources (CPU cores, GPU count).
main_assumptions: The core engine assumes that assignment triggers the necessary evaluation across the lattice; performance comparisons highlight differences between pencil vs. slab decomposition strategies for DFTs.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate scaling behavior for $SU(2)$ YM fields on GPUs, comparing TempLat to HILA; Figure 7 benchmarks ParaFaFT's FFT performance against established libraries (FFTW3/cuFFTMp) across various parallelization schemes.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the framework by detailing its mathematical abstraction capabilities and hardware portability. It then demonstrates applications through benchmarking diverse physical systems, including scalar field dynamics ($\phi^4$) and gauge theories ($SU(2)$ YM), culminating in detailed performance analyses of core components like DFTs.
why_interesting: While focused on lattice QFT, the underlying technology—a highly portable, expression-template-based framework for massively parallel computation—is directly relevant to simulating complex quantum many-body systems beyond standard Hamiltonians.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Left: Cached memory access: each thread gets a block of memory it walks through, allowing it to both cache the memory and enable SIMD. Right: Coalesced memory access, where a warp of threads walks through the memory. Each thread in the warp thus has a fixed stride when iterating. For illustration we show warp sizes of 8, but NVIDIA hardware typically has warp sizes of 32, while AMD wavefronts are 32 or 64 wide.
